title: How Long, LORD?
sum: Habakkuk opens by shouting at God. He cries "Violence!" and God does not save. He sees wickedness, ruin and quarreling, the law goes numb, and justice comes out twisted. This is not a message to a people. It is a prophet talking to God, in public, and the book keeps it that way.

God answers, and the answer is worse than the problem. He is raising up the Chaldeans, a fast and fierce nation that takes lands that are not its own and makes its strength its god. The prophet does not accept it. He reminds God that he is holy, that his eyes are too clean to approve evil, and asks why he is silent while the wicked swallow people more righteous than they are. The chapter ends with a net and a question no one answers yet.
readings: The setting is Judah in the last years of the 600s BC, under Jehoiakim. Josiah is dead, Babylon has beaten Egypt at Carchemish, and Judah's courts have gone bad. The Chaldeans are the real army that will come down on Jerusalem (2 Kings 24:1-2). Habakkuk's two complaints are the questions of a man who sees his country corrupt at home and doomed from outside.
Read as a pattern of prayer

The chapter follows the shape of a lament: a cry (1:2-4), an answer (1:5-11), a second protest (1:12-17). It lets believers do what Habakkuk does: speak to God honestly about injustice, with the creed in one hand (1:12) and the evidence in the other (1:13).
Read as a problem of evil

The question is old: a holy God uses a wicked power to correct his own people, and then does nothing while that power swallows nations. The Bible's answer comes by stages. Here there is only the question, and the book forces readers to feel its weight before it moves on.

views.H: Josiah died at Megiddo in 609 BC. Jehoiakim ruled until 598. Babylon beat Egypt at Carchemish in 605 and its army reached the coast of Philistia by 604. Judah's king served Nebuchadnezzar and then rebelled (2 Kings 24:1). The book does not name the king, so the dating rests on 1:6 and on the courts of 1:4. An earlier date, in Josiah's reign, and a later one, with the Greeks, are held by a few.
views.C: Who are the wicked of 1:4 and 1:13: Judeans, Assyrians, Babylonians? The chapter can be read as two rounds of a single dispute or as two layers added together. The Qumran commentary quotes 1:5 with "traitors" and the Greek has "scoffers"; both may reflect a Hebrew word that looks like "among the nations." The tradition about 1:12 ("we will not die" as a scribal change from "you do not die") is a rabbinic claim about an older text, not a manuscript reading.
views.J: The Talmud pictures Habakkuk as a man standing his ground before God (Bavli Taanit 23a). The rabbinic note on 1:12, that the scribes changed "you do not die" to "we will not die," is the best-known piece of Jewish discussion of the chapter (Mekhilta).
views.X: Acts 13:41 quotes 1:5 in the Greek as a warning about the news of Jesus. Later churches argued about evil from 1:13: Augustine's account of evil as the lack of a good, the Reformers' hidden and revealed will of God, and Wesley's stress on human freedom are set side by side in the card below.
views.F: Later interpreters could apply the Chaldeans to a final persecuting empire (compare Revelation 13), though the text itself speaks of Babylon. Most Christian and Jewish commentators see the chapter as describing events of the prophet's own day, with later use as a pattern.

deep.b: Hebrew prophets speak God's word to the people. Habakkuk speaks the people's word to God, and God replies. Moses, Jeremiah and Job do something like this, and the Psalms are full of it. The difference is that Habakkuk's book is built from that conversation. The first complaint (1:2-4) is about violence he can see. The answer (1:5-11) is a surprise. The second complaint (1:12-17) is about the answer. The structure is a dialogue in which the prophet has the last word before the watch of chapter 2.

The portrait of the nation in 1:6-11 is the most vivid war poem in the Twelve: leopards, wolves, eagles, laughing at kings, heaping dirt to take fortresses. It echoes Deuteronomy 28:49-50. It also stresses that this nation is its own law (1:7) and its own god (1:11). The Chaldean power is God's tool and also a guilty one, and the poem refuses to merge those two facts. Isaiah says the same of Assyria (Isaiah 10:5-15).

deep.title: Claude's theory: 1:12 "we will not die" is a deliberate hinge
deep.b: Claude's theory. Whether or not the scribes ever changed this line, as the rabbis say, the Masoretic "we will not die" does work in the book. It comes straight before the cry that God is using a wicked nation as a rod (1:12b), and the prophet asserts survival before he asserts a complaint. The line is a statement of faith that sits in the middle of the argument, like "yet I will rejoice" at the end (3:18). Other commentators also treat 1:12 as the book's first confession. This reading rests on 1:12, 2:4 and 3:18.

echoes: Psalm 13:1-2; Psalm 94:3; Jeremiah 12:1; Job 19:7; Deuteronomy 28:49-50; Isaiah 10:5-15; Genesis 18:25; Acts 13:41; 2 Kings 24:1-2

settings.to: the LORD, in the hearing of the worshippers who would read or sing it
settings.when: Probably in Jehoiakim's reign (609-598 BC), when Judah's courts were failing and Babylon was rising; the book gives no date
settings.why: To say aloud what the faithful in Judah were thinking: that God was deaf to violence and the law had stopped working. The prophet speaks for the victims. Knowing it is a prayer, not a sermon, changes the reading: the book begins by giving believers leave to ask God why.
settings.readers: Later readers in the exile and after, who had seen the Chaldeans come, found their own cry in the book and the answer that came back.
views: A common view (for example Roberts): the wicked are Judeans who pervert justice in the courts under Jehoiakim; Jeremiah 22:13-17 describes the same.
A minority reads the wicked as Assyrians or Egyptians in Josiah's time, so that the Chaldeans in 1:6 are a relief before they are a threat.
The Qumran commentary reads the wicked as the Wicked Priest and the righteous as the Teacher of Righteousness. That is a later community's reading.

settings.what: The LORD's answer: the Chaldeans are coming
settings.by: The LORD, speaking through the prophet
settings.to: Habakkuk and, in the plural "you," the community of Judah
settings.when: In reply to the first complaint, in the same days; the Chaldean power is rising
settings.why: To tell Habakkuk and Judah that God is not idle: he is at work, and the work is terrible. The answer is a shock, not a comfort. It tells the hearers that the judgment of 1:4 is coming from the outside, and that it will be a nation that has its own idea of justice.
settings.readers: For readers after 586 BC, the passage showed that the destruction had been foretold and was no sign of God's absence.
views: The rise of Babylon is still a surprise to Judah (the Hebrew verb is "I am about to raise").
The nation is already on the march, and the oracle explains what Judah has seen at Carchemish.

settings.why: To press the argument: if God is holy and eternal, how can he use a guilty nation to correct his own, and then watch it fish for people like a net? This is the central question of the book.
settings.readers: For the later community, the second complaint gave the right to question even God's answers.
views: The second complaint is aimed at the Chaldeans
The net-fisher of 1:14-17 is the Babylonian power, and the question is why God lets it go on (the common reading).
Some readers take the fisher more widely, as any violent power, including Judah's own rulers of 1:4.

traditions.q: If God is good and rules everything, why does he let the wicked prosper and swallow the righteous?
views: God permits evil because he respects the freedom of angels and human beings and can bring good out of it; he is never the cause of moral evil, directly or indirectly (Catechism 311). Evil is the lack of a good that should be present, in Augustine's account. No quick answer is enough: "only the Christian faith as a whole" is the answer (Catechism 309).

God is not the author of evil. Evil has no being of its own: it is a distortion of the freedom God gave. Basil the Great wrote a homily with that title. Orthodox writers commonly point to the cross and the resurrection rather than a theoretical solution (a summary of the emphasis, not a quotation).

Luther taught that God works all things in all, even in the wicked, yet is not to be blamed; behind the God who is revealed lies a hidden God whom we must not probe, and the cross is where God shows himself. The Formula of Concord denies that God is the cause of sin.

God has ordained whatever comes to pass, and yet he is not the author of sin, and no violence is done to the will of creatures (Westminster Confession 3.1). His providence reaches to the fall and to all sins, but the sinfulness comes only from the creature (5.4).
Wesley rejected the idea that God decrees sin or damnation. Evil comes from the misuse of the freedom God gives, God's love goes out to all, and he works through grace to turn people back.

Baptists are divided. Particular Baptists follow the Second London Confession (1689) on providence, which repeats the Westminster Confession; General Baptists and others hold that God foresees and permits sin without decreeing it.

title: Write the Vision
sum: Habakkuk climbs to his watch and waits for God to answer. The LORD tells him to write the vision on tablets so plainly that a runner can read it. It has an appointed time, it will not lie, and if it seems slow, he is to wait. Then comes the verse that Paul and Hebrews will quote: the proud person is not upright inside, but the righteous will live by his faithfulness.

The rest of the chapter is a song of five woes. The nations the plunderer has robbed will sing a taunt: woe to the one who piles up what is not his, who gets rich by wrong, who builds a city with blood, who shames his neighbor with wine, who trusts in a carved image. In the middle is the promise that the earth will be filled with the knowledge of the LORD's glory (2:14). The chapter ends in silence: the LORD is in his holy temple.
readings: Babylon will be paid back by the peoples it plundered. The five woes have the detail of an empire's habits: forced labor, loot, drunken feasts, idols. The prophet expects the fall of the oppressor in his own time or soon after (compare Jeremiah 50-51).
Read as a call to faithful waiting

The verse about the righteous living by faithfulness is the center. The proud are puffed up and the righteous are steady. The answer to Habakkuk's complaint is not an explanation but a way to live until the vision arrives.
Read as Scripture for the church

Paul reads 2:4 as the Scripture behind righteousness by faith (Romans 1:17; Galatians 3:11). Hebrews reads 2:3-4 as a call to endure until the coming one arrives (Hebrews 10:37-38). The Talmud reads it as the point to which the 613 commandments come back (Makkot 24a).

views.H: The woes use the common ancient habits of conquerors: loot, tribute, forced labor on building projects, drunken feasts, and felling forests. The plunderer is most often taken as Babylon, but Jehoiakim (Jeremiah 22:13-17) and Assyria have also been proposed. Babylon fell to Cyrus in 539 BC; whether that fulfills the woes is debated.
views.C: 2:4 is the most disputed verse in the book: the Hebrew 'uppelah occurs only here, the Greek reads "if he shrinks back," the pronoun varies from "his" (Hebrew) to "my" (Greek) to nothing (Paul). The Qumran commentary reads 2:5 with "wealth" for "wine." The structure of the woes, with the refrain at 2:8 and 2:17, is also argued.
views.J: Makkot 23b-24a ends the reduction of the commandments from 613 to one with Habakkuk's verse. Sanhedrin 97b uses 2:3 against date-calculators.
views.X: Romans 1:17 and Galatians 3:11 quote 2:4 for righteousness by faith; Hebrews 10:37-38 quotes 2:3-4 in the Greek for endurance. Luther said (in his 1545 preface to his Latin writings) that the "righteousness of God" in Romans 1:17 opened scripture to him, and Trent and the Reformers differ on what the verse says about justification (see the card). Hebrews 10:37 itself reads 2:3 of Christ's coming.
views.F: 2:3 ("it will surely come") and 2:14 ("the earth will be filled with the knowledge of the glory of the LORD") are taken by premillennial, amillennial and postmillennial readers as pointers to the end; they differ on when and how (see the card).

deep.b: Habakkuk 2:4 is quoted in three New Testament books and discussed by the Talmud. In Habakkuk the contrast is between the proud and the faithful; "faithfulness" ('emunah) is steadiness under pressure. Paul quotes it without a pronoun to say that the righteous live out of faith (Romans 1:17; Galatians 3:11). Hebrews quotes the Greek, with "my righteous one," to say that faith endures to the end. The rabbis find in it the center of the commandments. Each use is a real use of the verse; none replaces the others.

The five woes (2:6-8, 9-11, 12-14, 15-17, 18-20) each name a crime and then give its punishment, often in a pun on the crime. The one who piles up pledges is bitten by his creditors (2:6-7). The one who builds a nest on high is exposed by his own walls (2:9-11). The one who builds with blood sees fire eat the labor (2:12-13). The one who gets his neighbor drunk to shame him must drink the cup himself (2:15-16). The one who makes silent idols is told to be silent himself (2:19-20). Isaiah 5 has a similar run of woes.

echoes: Isaiah 8:1; Isaiah 21:6-8; Isaiah 11:9; Numbers 14:21; Jeremiah 51:58; Micah 3:10; Zephaniah 1:7; Zechariah 2:13; Romans 1:17; Galatians 3:11; Hebrews 10:35-39

settings.why: To show a prophet who will not leave until God replies. It gives the community a model of waiting for an answer.
settings.readers: Later readers, such as the rabbis, took it as a model of persistence in prayer (Bavli Taanit 23a).

settings.what: The LORD's answer: write the vision
settings.to: Habakkuk, and through him the readers of the tablets
settings.when: In reply to the prophet at the watch
settings.why: To tell Habakkuk and Judah that the answer is real, will be fulfilled in its time, and must be written down so that it can be read and checked. It tells the faithful what to do in the meantime: live steadily, as the proud do not.
settings.readers: For the exiles, this was the promise that the story was still moving to an end. For Paul and the writer of Hebrews, it is a sentence about the way God's people live between promise and fulfillment.
views: The vision is the downfall of the oppressor in 2:6-20 (a common reading).
A word about the final age
The Qumran commentary: God told Habakkuk what would come in the last generation but not the time, which he revealed to the Teacher.
A word about the coming one
The Greek and Hebrews 10:37: the vision is a person who will come.

settings.what: A taunt song with five woes
settings.by: The nations the plunderer has robbed, as the LORD says they will speak (2:6)
settings.to: The plunderer, probably the Chaldean empire, and through him any empire that lives by loot
settings.when: In the future of the oracle: when the robbed rise up (2:7)
settings.why: To tell the oppressed that their wrongs will be paid back and to tell the oppressor that his crimes are the cause of his fall. The woe form was the cry at a funeral, so the song announces the plunderer's death while he is alive. It answers 1:17: the net will not go on emptying forever.
settings.readers: For the exiles, the song was a promise that Babylon would not last.
views: The nations and the peoples of 2:5 and 2:8 are those Babylon conquered (the common reading).
The woes of 2:9-12 fit the charge in Jeremiah 22:13-17.
The Qumran commentary applies the woes to the Wicked Priest of the community's history.

traditions.q: What does "the righteous will live by faith" (Habakkuk 2:4; Romans 1:17) say about how a person is made right with God?
views: Faith is the beginning of justification, "the foundation and root" of it, but a person is justified by grace through faith and inward renewal, so that charity and good works increase the righteousness received (Council of Trent, session 6, chapters 7-8). Faith alone, without hope and love, does not justify.

Sinners are justified freely, for Christ's sake, through faith, when they believe that they are received into favor and their sins forgiven for his sake (Augsburg Confession, article 4). Luther said (in his 1545 preface to his Latin writings) that the "righteousness of God" in Romans 1:17 opened scripture to him.

Justification is God's free act: he pardons and accepts sinners, counting Christ's righteousness as theirs, and faith is the only means by which it is received, though it is never alone in the person justified (Westminster Confession, chapter 11).
We are accounted righteous before God only for the merit of Christ, by faith, not for our works; faith alone is a most wholesome doctrine (Thirty-Nine Articles, article 11).

Wesley taught justification by faith alone as God's pardon in Christ, followed by new birth and growth in holiness; faith is trust that works through love, and Christ's righteousness is imputed to believers for pardon.

The East does not frame the matter in terms of a legal declaration. Salvation is union with God and the healing of human nature. The Confession of Dositheus (1672, decree 13) denies that a person is justified by faith alone, and holds that faith works through love. The Orthodox Church's Old Testament is the Septuagint, which reads "my faithfulness" at this line.

Justification is God's full acquittal, on the principles of his righteousness, of all who repent and believe in Christ (Baptist Faith and Message 2000, article 4). Baptists commonly stress faith alone and personal trust.

traditions.q: What does each tradition teach about the course of history before the end, which readers then apply to Habakkuk 2:14 ("the earth will be filled with knowing the glory of the LORD")?
views: The Church awaits the final triumph; the kingdom will be fulfilled not by a historic triumph of the Church but by God's victory over the last unleashing of evil (Catechism 677). The Catechism does not comment on Habakkuk 2:14; applied to it, this implies that the filling of the earth is completed by God's act and not reached by history alone (an inference, not the Church's statement).

The Augsburg Confession (article 17) rejects "Jewish opinions" that before the resurrection of the dead the godly will take the kingdom of the world while the ungodly are suppressed; it is aimed at one kind of expected earthly kingdom, not at hope for the world to come. It does not discuss Habakkuk 2:14; applied to it, this implies that the fullness is looked for at Christ's return and the new creation (an inference).

Reformed teaching is divided. Postmillennial writers expect the gospel to fill the earth before Christ returns, and the Westminster Larger Catechism teaches Christians to pray that the gospel be spread throughout the world (question 191). Some amillennial Reformed writers apply 2:14 to the church's mission now, completed at the new creation.

Classic dispensationalists such as Lewis Sperry Chafer hold that the knowledge of the LORD will fill the earth in the thousand-year kingdom after Christ's return, when Israel is restored and the nations are ruled from Jerusalem. That is their general scheme; applied to 2:14, it puts the filling in the kingdom after the return.

The Fundamental Beliefs describe a thousand years in heaven after Christ's return and the earth made new when they end (belief 27). The statement does not discuss 2:14; applied to it, this implies that the filling comes after, not before, the return (an inference).

The Orthodox Church has no defined doctrine of a thousand-year kingdom. The Creed confesses of Christ that "his kingdom will have no end," and the Church sees the glory of God already revealed in Christ and in the liturgy while awaiting the general resurrection and the age to come.

title: A Prayer and a Song
sum: The last chapter is a psalm. Habakkuk prays that the LORD will do again in his own time what he did long ago, and remember compassion in his anger. Then the poem pictures the LORD marching up from Teman and Mount Paran, with plague in front and fever behind. Mountains break, the sea is trampled, sun and moon stand still, and the nations are threshed. He goes out to rescue his people and his anointed one.

The prophet's body shakes with fear. He will wait quietly for the day of trouble. And then comes the end of the book: even if the fig tree does not bud, and the vines, olives, fields, flock and herd all fail, he will exult in the LORD. The LORD is his strength, and makes his feet like a doe's. The book ends with a musician's note.
readings: Albright, Cross and Hiebert have argued that the poem is built from very old language, like Deuteronomy 33, Judges 5 and Psalm 68. If so, the book's last chapter is an older song that the prophet or an editor took up as his answer.

The prayer shows the prophet's reaction to the vision: he trembles, waits and rejoices. The answer to 1:2 is not an explanation but an appearance of God, and a promise that he will live in the middle of the trouble.

The poem has the marks of liturgy: a title, three selahs, a note for the music director. It is part of the Jewish festival of Shavuot and of the Christian canticles. It has been sung for centuries as a statement of joy under loss.

views.H: The poem pictures the march of the LORD from the south, as in the exodus and conquest poems. Cushan and Midian (3:7) belong to the wilderness years. The "day of trouble" (3:16) is probably the Chaldean attack. The harvest failure of 3:17 fits any war.
views.C: Chapter 3 is in the Greek and in Mur88 of the Twelve; the Qumran commentary stops at 2:20. Many scholars date the poem to the early monarchy or earlier (Albright, Cross, Hiebert); others see it as composed with the book. The hard words (3:2, 4, 5, 9, 14) have Greek forms that differ widely from the Hebrew.
views.J: Habakkuk 3 is the haftarah on the second day of Shavuot in the Diaspora (Bavli Megillah 31a). The rabbis play on 3:6 (halikhot 'olam, read halakhot; Bavli Megillah 28b).
views.X: The poem is Ode 4 of the Greek canticles, and a canticle of Lauds in the Roman rite. The Greek "two living things" (3:2) led later writers to the ox and the ass at the manger and to the two Testaments. Luke 1:47 echoes 3:18.
views.F: The march of the LORD, the shaking of the earth and the threshing of the nations are used in later Jewish and Christian writing as a picture of the final day of the LORD; the text itself uses the past tense of the exodus and conquest as well as the future of the prophet's own day.

deep.b: Chapter 3 has some of the hardest Hebrew in the Bible. 3:2 ("in the middle of the years"), 3:4 ("rays" or "horns"), 3:5 (Plague and Resheph), 3:9 (the oaths and the arrows) and 3:13-14 all have more than one reading. The Greek often differs from the Hebrew. The Plain follows the Hebrew and puts the other readings in the variants. Do not let the hard words hide the movement of the poem: prayer (3:2), arrival (3:3-7), battle (3:8-15), fear (3:16), joy (3:17-19).

The LORD comes from the south, on horses and chariots, with arrows and spear, and the sea and rivers shake. The picture is of the divine warrior known from Exodus 15, Judges 5, Deuteronomy 33 and Psalm 68, and in the poems of Canaan. In Habakkuk the battle is for the LORD's people and anointed (3:13), and the prophet is not a fighter but a watcher. The poem ends not with a victory shout but with a vow of joy while the fields are empty.

echoes: Exodus 15; Deuteronomy 33:2; Judges 5:4-5; Psalm 68:7-8; Psalm 77:16-20; Joshua 10:12-13; 2 Samuel 22:34; Deuteronomy 32:13; Deuteronomy 33:29; Luke 1:47

settings.what: A prayer of Habakkuk and the march of the LORD
settings.to: the LORD, for the singing congregation (the heading and the note to the music director)
settings.when: After the vision of chapter 2; the poem itself may be much older than the prophet
settings.why: To ask the LORD to act again as he acted at the exodus and Sinai, and to remember compassion. The prophet takes the memory of the LORD's march as the ground of his hope. Knowing it was sung in worship changes the reading: it is the community's prayer as well as one man's.
settings.readers: For the exiles and later worshippers, it was the song to sing when the LORD seemed far away.
views: An old hymn adopted by the prophet
Albright, Cross and Hiebert: the poem is early and was taken into the book.
Part of the prophet's own work
Others: the prayer is the book's answer to the dialogue and was composed or shaped with it.

settings.what: The prophet's trembling and his vow of joy
settings.to: himself, the LORD and the congregation
settings.when: After hearing the report of the LORD's coming and before the day of trouble
settings.why: To show how a believer lives between the promise and its keeping: afraid, waiting quietly, and giving thanks even if everything the land produces is gone. It answers the question of 1:2 with a posture and not a solution.
settings.readers: For the later community, it is the vow to say when the covenant curses of Deuteronomy have come true.
views: The day of trouble is Babylon's attack
The day of trouble is the day of the LORD
The later Jewish and Christian reading, in which the prophet waits for the final day.
